strengths: Clear and meaningful problem: solving two-player zero-sum differential games with one-sided payoff information and continuous actions, states, and time is a genuine gap; existing IIEFG solvers (CFR+, FTRL/MMD variants) scale with the discretized action space, and the paper explains why this is fundamentally mismatched with differential games satisfying Isaacs' condition (pure/atomic equilibria).

Solid theoretical development building on rigorous literature (Aumann-Maschler 'Cav u' theorem, De Meyer's dual game, Cardaliaguet 2007/2009): Theorem 4.1 (I-atomic / (I+1)-atomic equilibrium strategies via a pushforward-measure/convexification argument) is an elegant reformulation that removes action-space size from the per-infostate minimax problems; the proof of Thm. 3.1 completes a sketch in Cardaliaguet (2009).

The connection between value convexification and equilibrium is well explained (Sec. 4, Fig. 2, App. C-E), including worked analytical examples (repeated normal-form games, zero-sum beer-quiche, Hexner's game) that make the primal-dual machinery concrete and verifiable.

The multigrid/FAS extension to backward induction with value networks is a novel and sensible adaptation from PDE solving, addressing the exponential error-propagation issue identified in Theorem 4.2; runtime improvements (2-4x) are demonstrated.

Empirical comparisons against appropriate SOTA baselines (CFR+, MMD, DeepCFR, CFR-BR-Primal, and the continuous-action JPSPG) on a game with a known analytical equilibrium, showing CAMS is invariant to action-space discretization while baselines degrade, and producing strategies closer to ground truth than DeepCFR and JPSPG.

Reasonably comprehensive appendix: complexity analysis of existing solvers (App. F), NTK-based error propagation analysis (App. G), full algorithm pseudocode, and experimental details/hyperparameters.
Impact statement is present and thoughtful.
weaknesses: Evaluation is essentially confined to one game family (variants of Hexner's game). While the analytical equilibrium makes this a strong testbed, no second environment (e.g., a different dynamics class or payoff structure) is used, so generality of the claimed scalability advantage beyond this family remains unvalidated.

The practical solver has no end-to-end convergence guarantee: Theorem 4.1 assumes exact global minimax solutions, but the implementation uses DS-GDA on nonconvex-nonconcave problems with only a worst-case O(eps^-4) generic bound; local saddle points could corrupt the value networks, and no analysis or empirical evidence is given on how often DS-GDA finds global solutions for these specific problems.

The multigrid approach is purely heuristic in the game setting: FAS corrections are fitted with neural networks without error bounds or convergence theory for the nonlinear HJI-systems arising here; the resulting value/strategy approximation quality is assessed only qualitatively (e.g., P1's reveal time 0.60s vs. ground truth 0.5s is a ~20% error, and P2's dual approximation is acknowledged to be worse).

Reported compute is heavy (17-46 hours on a single A100/H100 even for 4-16 step games with small I), which tempers the 'scalable' claim; scalability is only demonstrated up to 3D/6D actions, 16 time steps, and I=2 types, while complexity scales as O(I^2) or worse in the number of types.

Some comparisons have fairness/clarity issues: different NashConv thresholds for CAMS (1e-5) vs. baselines (1e-3), differently sized DeepCFR configurations, and 'similar compute' comparisons that are hard to verify precisely; error bars and variance over seeds are largely absent (only one std figure for tr).

Positioning relative to Ghimire et al. (2024) - the closest prior work, which already established value existence and a constrained-game framework for this game class - could better delineate what is new beyond the atomic-strategy reformulation and multigrid; the incremental nature of the delta is not fully dissected.

Restricted scope due to assumptions (Isaacs' condition, one-sided payoff information only, small number of types, perfect recall, fully observable states) is acknowledged but limits applicability; no discussion of what fails when Isaacs' condition does not hold.
Reproducibility: no explicit statement of code release; several minor typos and presentation lapses (e.g., duplicated contribution statements, notation overload) reduce polish.

strengths: The paper builds on a rigorous theoretical foundation (Cardaliaguet's primal-dual DP framework) and the splitting reformulation (Thm 4.1) showing equilibrium strategies are I-atomic is an elegant observation that directly explains why discretization-based IIEFG solvers scale poorly on this game class.
Validation is done against Hexner's game, which admits an analytical Nash equilibrium, allowing quantitative evaluation of strategy error rather than only self-play metrics.

Comparisons include a relevant continuous-action baseline (JPSPG) alongside discretized CFR+/MMD/DeepCFR, and the empirical invariance of CAMS cost to action-space size supports the central complexity claim.
The extension of multigrid/FAS to the backward-induction structure of these games is a reasonable engineering contribution, with consistent (if modest) runtime reductions reported.

The paper is honest in places about its limitations, e.g., acknowledging the exponential dependence on time steps in Thm 4.2 and that the Cav-u convexification idea originates in Aumann–Maschler/De Meyer.
weaknesses: The claimed scalability is not convincingly demonstrated. Solving a 2D, 16-step game takes ~46 hours on a single H100 GPU (even with multigrid: ~18 hours). For a paper whose title and thesis center on scalability, the absolute runtimes are large, and the empirical scaling study covers only 4/10/16 time steps of one low-dimensional linear game.

Evaluation scope is very narrow: essentially one game family (Hexner's game, linear dynamics, I=2 types) in all experiments. No results on any of the motivating attack-defense scenarios beyond pursuit games, and the 3D 'high-dimensional' experiment is purely qualitative with no quantitative error or runtime analysis.

Theoretical novelty is limited. Thm 3.1 completes a proof sketch from Cardaliaguet (2009); the atomic/splitting structure of Thm 4.1 is largely the known Cav-u/concavification theory of Aumann–Maschler and De Meyer translated to the differential setting, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

The overall pipeline lacks end-to-end guarantees. The minimax subproblems are solved with DS-GDA (O(ε^-4) worst-case, no last-iterate guarantee on the nonconvex-nonconcave objectives actually solved), and the neural value approximation has exponential-in-K complexity (Thm 4.2). It is therefore unclear how close the returned strategies are to equilibrium in general settings.

Baseline comparisons are potentially unfair or under-tuned: discretized CFR+/MMD are applied to a problem they are known to handle poorly, convergence thresholds differ across algorithms (10^-5 for CAMS vs 10^-3 for baselines), and the 4-stage comparisons are made under 'similar compute' approximations rather than equal-budget protocols. No tuning sensitivity is reported.

The constrained-game variant relies on a heuristic penalty and an approximated safe zone following Ghimire et al. (2024), with no guarantees and no quantitative evaluation of the resulting strategies.

P2's (dual) strategy, a core contribution, is validated only qualitatively; the paper notes higher approximation error in the dual game but does not quantify it or assess equilibrium quality of the full primal-dual pair.

No code or reproduction details sufficient to reproduce the results are promised, and the multigrid speedup (~2–3x) is reported without comparison to alternative accelerations (e.g., warm-starting without multigrid, coarser-to-fine baselines).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and under-explored gap: solvers for two-player zero-sum differential games with one-sided incomplete information and continuous actions, states, and time, where existing IIEFG solvers (CFR variants, FTRL/MMD) require discretization and scale poorly with action-space size.

The key structural insight (Thm. 4.1) that equilibrium strategies are I-atomic (resp. (I+1)-atomic) under Isaacs' condition is well-motivated, connects cleanly to the Cav u/convexification theory of Aumann-Maschler and De Meyer, and leads to a formulation whose complexity is decoupled from the action-space size.

The primal-dual decomposition for recovering both players' strategies is clearly presented, with useful pedagogical material (Appendices C-E) connecting value convexification, approachability, and Nash equilibrium construction.

The empirical comparison against CFR+, MMD, DeepCFR, CFR-BR-Primal, and the continuous-action solver JPSPG is appropriate and shows the expected invariance of CAMS to action-space size, with favorable wall-time and action-error results on games with analytical ground truth.

The multigrid (FAS) extension for backward-induction value approximation is a sensible adaptation of classical multigrid ideas to incomplete-information HJI equations, and yields a substantial (2-3x) runtime reduction in the reported experiments.

The appendix is thorough: proofs, analytical examples (Hexner's game via primal-dual formulation, a turn-based beer-quiche variant), and algorithmic details support the main claims and improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is partly incremental relative to prior theory: the primal/dual DPs, existence results (Thm. 3.1), and the splitting/convexification structure are largely due to Cardaliaguet (2007, 2009) and Ghimire et al. (2024); multigrid for HJB/HJI is also well-established (Han & Wan, 2013). The main new contributions are the atomicity reformulation for scalable solving and the engineering of the neural multigrid solver, which is a solid but not groundbreaking combination.

The proof of Thm. 3.1 in App. A uses a second-order Taylor expansion of V (requiring C^2 smoothness / L1-smoothness of the value function and well-defined Hessians at collocation points), but the stated assumptions A1-A4 only guarantee Lipschitz continuity; the value function of such games is generally non-smooth. This gap in the proof needs to be addressed or the theorem restated under stronger assumptions.

Evaluation is confined to a single game family (variants of Hexner's game) with I=2 types and low-dimensional state spaces (2D/3D); the 'high-dimensional' scalability demo is only a 6D action space. Scalability claims would be more convincing with more diverse dynamics, more types, and larger state dimensions.

Baseline comparisons have fairness concerns: different NashConv stopping thresholds are used for CAMS (1e-5) versus baselines (1e-3), baselines must operate on discretized action sets while CAMS works natively in continuous space, and no exploitability/NashConv metric is reported for the 10- and 16-stage games where the analytical equilibrium is unavailable (only qualitative trajectory comparisons and the concealment time statistic).

Absolute runtimes are large (9-46 hours on a single H100/A100 for up to 16 time steps), which somewhat tempers the 'scalable solver' claim; no ablation on the sensitivity to the DS-GDA solver's nonconvexity, collocation sample size N, or neural value-approximation quality is provided despite Thm. 4.2 highlighting exponential error propagation (C^T) as the main bottleneck.

The theoretical complexity result (Thm. 4.2 / G.4) relies on strong NTK-based assumptions (infinitely wide networks, positive-definite kernel) and a constant C that is not controlled for neural nets, as the authors themselves acknowledge; the practical relevance of this bound is limited.
No mention of code release or reproducibility artifacts in the manuscript.
Writing has minor issues (typos such as 'uniformed player', inconsistent notation between U the non-revealing value and U the action set in Sec. 4/5), which occasionally impede readability.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated theoretical contribution: the paper extends the known atomic equilibrium structure of one-sided-information repeated games (Aumann–Maschler, De Meyer) to differential games, proving I-atomic (resp. (I+1)-atomic) equilibrium strategies via a convexification argument, with a fairly complete proof in the appendix (Thm 4.1, Thm 4.2 with quadratic consistency lemmas).

The primal/dual DP reformulations (P1, P2) give a concrete, computable characterization with an approximation guarantee (error O((T-t)τ)), which is a genuinely useful bridge between HJ PDE theory and learning-based game solving.

Comprehensive validation across three learning modes (value approximation, model-free MARL, MPC) against a reasonable set of SOTA baselines (CFR+, MMD, DeepCFR, JPSPG, PPO, R-NaD), with ground-truth NE available for Hexner's game, quantified action errors, U-invariance demonstration, and multigrid speedups (Table 1) with quantified runtime reductions (~2.5x).

Impressive application showcase: a differentiable 22-player football pursuit–evasion game (K=10, continuous actions) solved in ~30 minutes on a laptop, with plausible qualitative match to real tactical behavior (concealment window ~0.5s vs. reported ~1s).

The multigrid/FAS extension to the nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi equations underlying the primal and dual DPs is a sensible and practically effective engineering contribution, with the algorithm given in pseudocode.

Honest positioning: the paper clearly delineates what is inherited from Cardaliaguet (2007) and Ghimire et al. (2024) versus what is new, and explicitly acknowledges limitations (stochastic dynamics left as future work).
weaknesses: Narrow applicability of the theory: results require deterministic dynamics, Isaacs' condition, compact action sets, and one-sided payoff information with small I. The authors admit that with stochastic dynamics/observations the convex Bellman operators become only lower bounds and atomic NEs may fail, which limits the practical scope considerably.

The football demonstration — the headline result — has no quantitative evaluation: no baseline comparison (justified by scale, but alternatives like abstraction-based IIEFG solvers or self-play without the atomic prior are not attempted), and the validation is qualitative trajectory inspection plus an anecdotal comparison to a coaching blog. Solution quality/approximation gap for this game is unknown.

Evaluation is dominated by Hexner's game, a small benchmark with an analytic NE; all experiments use I=2. No experiments probe scaling in I, where complexity is still I^K — exponential in K — so the claimed scalability win is asymmetric (eliminates U but retains K-dependence).

The comparison with discrete baselines is somewhat foregone: CAMS directly hard-codes the proven equilibrium structure (I prototypes per type) while baselines must discover the full distribution over U actions. The paper does not test whether baselines with similarly informed parameterizations (e.g., prototype-based policy classes without the theory) would close the gap, making it unclear how much of the gain comes from the theorem versus simply constraining the hypothesis class.

Unresolved discrepancy with Rudolph et al. (2025): R-NaD performs much better here than in prior work, and the explanation is only a conjecture about non-interior equilibria; this weakens the MARL comparison.

Some claims overreach relative to evidence, e.g., 'significant improvements in learning accuracy and efficiency from SOTA IIEFG solvers' is only established on one small benchmark; the NashConv termination thresholds differ between CAMS (10^-5) and baselines (10^-3), complicating cost comparisons even if it favors baselines.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, several hyperparameters and solver details (DS-GDA settings, collocation sizes, network architectures for CAMS) are underspecified relative to the appendix detail given for baselines.

Theory novelty is somewhat incremental relative to Ghimire et al. (2024) and Cardaliaguet (2007): the value existence and primal-dual framework exist; the genuinely new pieces are the atomicity proof and the multigrid scheme, and the atomicity argument is a fairly direct transplant of the convexification/Cav-u machinery.

strengths: The theoretical core is coherent and non-trivial: the paper extends the known atomic equilibrium structure of one-sided-information repeated games (Aumann–Maschler; De Meyer; Cardaliaguet) to differential games, with primal/dual reformulations (Thm 4.1) and a discretization-error analysis (Thm 4.2) showing convergence of the atomic approximations to the NE of the continuous-time game.

The computational payoff of the theory is real: reducing game-tree complexity from U^2K to I^K / (I+1)^K genuinely enables solving problems (continuous actions, moderate K) that are out of reach for discretization-based IIEFG solvers, and the multigrid/FAS extension is a sensible acceleration.

Experiments are anchored to a game with an analytically known NE (Hexner's game), allowing quantitative evaluation of solution accuracy rather than only reward-based comparison, and the analysis in App. D on error propagation is a useful addition.
The paper is generally well written and honest about limitations (e.g., stochastic dynamics break the belief-control argument and are deferred to future work).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the theory: the atomic/Cav-u structure and the primal-dual reformulation are directly inherited from De Meyer (1996), Cardaliaguet (2007), and Ghimire et al. (2024); the authors themselves note that Cardaliaguet (2009) already sketched the recursion used in Thm 4.2. The genuinely new part (porting the structure into MARL/MPC pipelines) is more of an application-level observation than a fundamental contribution.

Evaluation is narrow: quantitative comparisons are performed essentially on a single toy benchmark (Hexner's game) with small I and simple linear dynamics. The headline 'solving football' result is qualitative only — no ground truth, no quantitative metrics, no baselines, and no validation that the smoothed 'merge' dynamics and clamping actually satisfy the assumptions (A1–A5, Isaacs' condition) needed for the theory to apply.

Comparison fairness is questionable: discrete baselines are run with a loose NashConv threshold (1e-3) while CAMS uses 1e-5, and JPSPG is run for 2e8 iterations; no hyperparameter search is reported for baselines, so the claimed superiority over SOTA solvers (CFR+, MMD, Deep-CFR, R-NaD, JPSPG) is weakly supported.

Practical significance is limited: wall-clock costs are high even for the toy game (17–46 GPU-hours on Hexner's game; Tab. 1), and the method requires known, deterministic, differentiable dynamics, Isaacs' condition, and small I (I^K and (I+1)^K rollouts). The class of applicable problems ('2p0s1') is quite narrow relative to the paper's framing.

Restrictive assumptions undermine the generality of the claims: deterministic dynamics are essential for precise belief control (acknowledged in the remarks), yet the abstract and introduction advertise broad applicability to sports, defense, cybersecurity, and finance without evidence.

Reproducibility and polish: no code release is mentioned; there are typos (e.g., '2p01s' vs '2p0s1', Fig. 6 labeled '(c)' twice), a citation with 'utm_source=chatgpt.com' in the URL, and an apparently extraneous reference (Amos et al., 2017; Jacot et al., 2018 appears only via NTK usage), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully finished.
The 0.5s vs. 1.0s 'concealment time' comparison to football coaching folklore is not a meaningful validation and is presented more prominently than it deserves.

strengths: The paper identifies a clean and practically important structural result: for 2p0s1 differential games, equilibrium behavioral strategies are I-atomic (P1) and (I+1)-atomic (P2) in continuous action spaces, collapsing the game-tree complexity from U^2K to I^K / (I+1)^K. This is a meaningful extension of the Cav-u / De Meyer dual results from repeated games to the differential-game setting.

The theory is presented with a coherent primal-dual framework (splitting reformulations P1 and P2), and the approximation result (Thm 4.2, with quadratic-in-tau consistency via semiconcavity and the convex-envelope Lipschitz lemma) is carefully worked out in the appendix, going beyond the recursion sketch in Cardaliaguet (2009).

The work is unusually complete in covering three usage modes: direct value approximation (CAMS with multigrid/FAS), model-free MARL (CAMS-DRL via PPO/MMD on atomic prototype parameterizations), and MPC (CAMS-MPC on the collapsed game tree). This breadth strengthens the claim that the structure is practically exploitable.

Experiments include a benchmark with an analytical ground-truth NE (Hexner's game), enabling quantitative evaluation of solution accuracy and U-invariance of compute, and demonstrate clear wins over strong baselines (CFR+, MMD, CFR-BR-Primal, DeepCFR, JPSPG, R-NaD) at comparable compute. The conjecture that PG methods struggle with non-interior (atomic) equilibria is a useful insight for the MARL community.

The 11-vs-11 differentiable football demonstration (I=2, K=10, continuous actions) is an ambitious end-to-end result: solvable in ~30 minutes on a laptop where the discretized IIEFG would have complexity ~10^440, and the learned concealment time (0.5s) qualitatively matches coaching heuristics (~1s).
weaknesses: Novelty of the core theory is incremental. The atomic equilibrium structure and the primal-dual/Cav-u machinery are well established for repeated games (Aumann et al., 1995; De Meyer, 1996), and the value-existence and discretization arguments rest heavily on Cardaliaguet (2007, 2009) and Ghimire et al. (2024). The authors themselves acknowledge Cardaliaguet (2009) provided the recursion underlying Thm 4.2. The main genuinely new elements are the atomicity statement for the discrete-time DPs and its algorithmic exploitation.

The setting is restrictive: deterministic dynamics, compact actions, Isaacs' condition, perfect observation, and small I. The remarks admit the method breaks down for stochastic dynamics/observations (convex Bellman operators become only lower bounds), and the resulting complexity I^K is still exponential in I. The class of tractable games is narrow relative to the framing (sports, defense, finance).

The football 'solving' claim requires the loose-bounds merge/clamp dynamics to satisfy Isaacs' condition (A4). The appendix argues the map is piecewise control-affine with almost-everywhere differentiable saturations, but a piecewise-affine, clamped system does not obviously satisfy the smooth Isaacs condition, and no verification of A4 for the actual game is given. The headline 22-player result is therefore only qualitatively supported.

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: CAMS is run to a stricter NashConv threshold (1e-5) than the baselines (1e-3); DeepCFR is given only 1000 (or 100) iterations while JPSPG gets 2e8; wall-time comparisons mix different hardware and stopping criteria. These choices may overstate the advantage of CAMS.

The value-approximation solver (DS-GDA on nonconvex-nonconcave minimax) has only local convergence guarantees, while the theory (Thm 4.2, 5.1) assumes exact or epsilon-exact minimax solutions; the gap between the guaranteed epsilon and what DS-GDA actually achieves in practice is not analyzed. The multigrid extension is empirical (Table 1) with no convergence theory, and Thm 5.1 itself shows complexity exponential in K.

The football evaluation is purely qualitative (no quantitative metric, no baseline, single scenario), and the calibration against a 'roughly one-second' coaching blog post (Grabowski, 2020) is weak evidence. Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is mentioned.
